stories.kick: International · Human rights · Press ✓ 6 outlets · sanction details still being confirmed
stories.hl: Nobel Peace Prize goes to South Africa's Navi Pillay. Hours later, the U.S. sanctioned the International Criminal Court
stories.dek: On the day a prize went to defend international legal bodies, the U.S. Treasury put one of those bodies on its sanctions list. South Korean stocks were off yesterday for the Hangeul Day trading holiday
body: On the 9th (local time), the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced, at 6 p.m. Korea time, that this year's Nobel Peace Prize goes to Navi Pillay (85), a South African jurist. She is also reported to be of Indian descent (Mint, Hindustan Times). She served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and as a judge of the International Criminal Court (ICC), and is now an ad hoc judge of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) (Yonhap, Reuters). According to The Washington Post, the committee cited her work in strengthening international legal institutions. Yonhap reported that the committee also criticized the U.S. sanctions on the ICC. It is the second year in a row that a woman has won. Pillay said she dedicated the prize to survivors of international crimes, and joked that if the applause went on, she would have to share the prize with President Trump. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa welcomed it as “a tribute to courage.” It is the first South African laureate since Mandela, 33 years ago. The UN also congratulated her, calling it a signal for human rights (Handelsblatt).

Reactions split at once. Israel's Foreign Ministry condemned the award, saying “Goebbels would cheer” (Yonhap, Kyunghyang Shinmun). President Trump has openly said he wants this prize (Yonhap). Forbes reported that Trump reposted a message calling the laureate “someone who hates America and Israel.” The same day, the U.S. Treasury announced it had put the ICC itself on its sanctions list (Reuters exclusive, NHK). In August the U.S. had sanctioned ICC President Tomoko Akane; now it has widened the pressure to the whole institution. Russia also demanded that the Netherlands hand over Akane and others (NHK, Japan Times). Der Spiegel noted that Pillay has criticized Israel's actions in the Gaza Strip, and Mexico's Expansión called it an award that Trump and Netanyahu would find uncomfortable. Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi voiced deep concern, saying it was incompatible with Japan's position (Asahi). With a former judge winning the prize on the day her court came under sanctions, the two events are read together. But whether the timing of the sanctions was linked to the award, and what exactly the sanctions cover, has not yet been confirmed. South Korea is an ICC member, so this is not someone else's problem. This weekend, the reactions of the ICC and European governments are the thing to watch.

popup.title: Nobel Peace Prize goes to South Africa's Navi Pillay. Hours later, the U.S. sanctioned the International Criminal Court
popup.what: On the 9th, the Norwegian Nobel Committee named Navi (Navanethem) Pillay (85) the winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. A South African jurist, she has served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights and as an ICC judge, and is now an ad hoc judge of the ICJ. The Washington Post reported that the committee cited her work in strengthening international legal institutions. Yonhap reported that the committee also criticized the U.S. sanctions on the ICC. Israel's Foreign Ministry condemned the award. Reuters reported exclusively that the U.S. sanctioned the ICC a few hours after the award, and NHK said the U.S. Treasury designated the ICC as a sanctions target. The specific effects of the designation are described differently from report to report, so we are still confirming them.
popup.why: In August the U.S. sanctioned ICC President Tomoko Akane; this time it targeted the institution itself. If an international court that tries war crimes comes under sanctions from major powers, investigations and trials themselves can be shaken. Reports also emerged that, the same day, Russia demanded that the Netherlands and others hand over President Akane (NHK, Japan Times). International legal institutions appear to be pressed from both sides.
popup.me: South Korea is an ICC member. The direct impact is small, but international law could become an issue in Korea–U.S. relations. As Japan's prime minister voiced concern, U.S. allies may be forced to take positions.
popup.a: The international bodies that judge war crimes must be protected. The prize is that signal, and the sanctions are political retaliation.
popup.b: The ICC has asserted jurisdiction over non-members such as the U.S. and Israel. The U.S. sees this as an infringement of sovereignty. One can argue that reading the timing of the award and the sanctions as one thing is excessive.
popup.say: A prize cannot stop sanctions. All that remains is the fact that sanctions came the day the prize was awarded. There are two things to watch next. Whether the sanctions go beyond the personal accounts and visas of ICC staff to block the court's operations, and whether European governments issue official positions. What remains unconfirmed is causation in the timing.

stories.kick: International · Security · Press ✓ 4 outlets · the attacker is per the Houthis' claim
stories.hl: Houthis' attack on Riyadh airport kills 3; another ship is hit in Hormuz
body: Saudi civil aviation authorities said three people died at Riyadh airport after an attack by the Houthis (Reuters, AP). The Houthis claimed responsibility; Saudi Arabia has not itself named who carried out the attack. Yonhap reported that the dead include a Saudia captain. Earlier, on the 7th, Saudi Arabia announced that three people died in attacks on the Riyadh and Abha airports; whether the two tallies refer to the same incident has not been confirmed. Lufthansa and Indian airlines suspended Riyadh routes, and the EU aviation authority widened its Saudi airspace warning (Reuters). The U.S. Treasury sanctioned Turkish, UAE and Indian companies involved in illicit trade in Iranian petroleum products (Yonhap). In the Strait of Hormuz, a ship was hit by a projectile on the 9th, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said, and the Revolutionary Guards said they would punish ships that break the shipping lane (Yonhap). Oil fell in Asian trading after President Trump spoke of negotiations with Iran (Reuters). On the 8th, New York WTI rose 3.6% to the $91 range. New York stocks opened higher on Friday as oil fell (Yonhap), but trading was still under way as this paper went to press, so we could not include the close.

stories.hl: SpaceX spectrum purchase sends telecom stocks sharply lower
stories.dek: After SpaceX, the Starlink operator, moved to buy spectrum, U.S. and European telecom stocks all slid on the 9th. Deutsche Telekom fell about 7%.

popup.kick: Telecom · Tech · Press ✓ 5 outlets · deal terms still being confirmed
popup.title: SpaceX spectrum purchase sends telecom stocks sharply lower
popup.what: Telecom stocks in the U.S. and Europe slid on the 9th on news that SpaceX will buy U.S. wireless spectrum (Reuters, CNA). Deutsche Telekom's shares fell about 7% (Reuters). The Financial Times reported that U.S. carriers lost $45 billion in market value, and MarketWatch reported that AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile shares fell. Bloomberg reported that Verizon and AT&T bonds were also weak. The purchase price and approval process could not be confirmed in these materials.
popup.why: This spectrum would underpin Starlink's mobile service. It reads as a signal that a satellite company will compete directly with mobile carriers.
popup.me: No news yet touches domestic carriers directly. It is a signal of whether direct satellite-to-phone competition is spreading worldwide.
popup.a: Direct satellite communication is a new competition that narrows dead zones. Consumers get more options.
popup.b: Investors may have overreacted earlier. Satellites have large limits in replacing terrestrial network capacity.
popup.say: Stocks moved before the contract did. Only when the contract terms and regulatory approval are out can we tell whether this drop was excessive.
popup.src: Reuters (telecom decline, Deutsche Telekom, 10/9) · CNA (10/9) · Financial Times (market-value loss, 10/9) · MarketWatch (10/9) · Bloomberg (bonds, 10/9)

stories.hl: Rep. Jung Chung-rae's U.S. visa put on hold. Foreign Ministry: “Inappropriate to link to Korea–U.S. relations”
stories.dek: The schedule for the parliamentary audit changed. The ruling Democratic Party of Korea expressed regret; the opposition People Power Party retorted that it is an ‘anomalous signal.’

popup.kick: Diplomacy · Politics · Press ✓ 4 outlets · reason for the visa decision not disclosed
popup.title: Rep. Jung Chung-rae's U.S. visa put on hold. Foreign Ministry: “Inappropriate to link to Korea–U.S. relations”
popup.what: The issuance of a U.S. visa to Rep. Jung Chung-rae of the Democratic Party of Korea has been put on hold, making it hard for him to attend the National Assembly Foreign Affairs and Unification Committee's parliamentary audit of overseas missions in the Americas. Jung switched his schedule to the audit in Europe (Dong-A Ilbo). The Democratic Party expressed deep regret and urged a quick resolution, while the People Power Party attacked it as an anomalous signal across diplomacy, intelligence and security. A Foreign Ministry official said linking an individual visa to Korea–U.S. relations as a whole is inappropriate, and that because visa review details are confidential under U.S. law, the facts are hard to verify (Kyunghyang Shinmun, Dong-A Ilbo). On Facebook, Jung asked people to refrain from extreme claims and remarks that harm the alliance.
popup.why: One visa case has spread into domestic politics and interpretations of Korea–U.S. relations. The government warns against over-reading it, but the opposition sees evidence of a rift.
popup.me: There is no confirmation that visa procedures for ordinary applicants have changed. Visas are reviewed case by case, so there is no basis for applying this case directly.
popup.a: Blocking a lawmaker's legislative work is inappropriate. Between allies, there should be courtesy.
popup.b: Visas are a matter of U.S. sovereignty. Blowing it up into a diplomatic issue without knowing the reason is hasty.
popup.say: The only known fact is the status ‘under review.’ It is neither a denial nor an approval. What to watch next is when the U.S. decides whether to issue it.
popup.src: Dong-A Ilbo, Kyunghyang Shinmun, Korea Economic Daily (10/9) · Yonhap (Foreign Ministry's and Jung's positions, 10/9)

stories.hl: President Lee's approval at 37%, Gallup Korea
stories.dek: Unchanged from the previous survey. Ruling-party support was 35%, the lowest since the current government took office.

popup.kick: Politics · Press ✓ 3 outlets · figures are from the Gallup Korea survey
popup.title: President Lee's approval at 37%, Gallup Korea
popup.what: In the regular survey Gallup Korea released on the 9th, positive evaluation of President Lee Jae-myung's job performance was 37%, unchanged from the previous survey. Negative evaluation fell 5 percentage points to 51% (SBS). In party support, the Democratic Party stood at 35%, the lowest since the current government took office (Yonhap). Maeil Business Newspaper also reported the result, citing the survey.
popup.why: If positive stayed the same while negative fell, the share of respondents giving no opinion may have grown. It should be read together with the fall in the ruling party's support.
popup.me: The current approval trend is the backdrop to the ruling–opposition fight during the parliamentary audit period.
popup.say: 37% is unchanged, but 51% fell. Whether no-opinion responses grew needs the survey's detailed data. The key is whether the direction continues in next week's survey.
popup.src: Yonhap, SBS, Maeil Business Newspaper (Gallup Korea survey, 10/9)

popup.title: Tech drags New York on Thursday; KOSPI is closed again today

The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield was 5.231%. Reuters cited concerns over AI investment costs and high interest rates. WTI rose 3.6% to the $91 range. New York stocks opened higher on Friday as oil fell (Yonhap), but trading was still under way as this paper went to press. The Korean market was closed on Friday for Hangeul Day. The KOSPI closed at 6,625.93 (−2.62%) on Thursday and the KOSDAQ at 892.27 (−0.69%).
popup.why: Overseas factors piled up while the Korean market was closed. They will all be reflected at once on the next trading day, Monday the 12th.
popup.me: Be prepared for volatility right after Monday's open. Friday's New York close will not come out until early Saturday morning.
popup.say: Friday's early rebound means something only once the close is known. How much of Thursday's tech slide it recovered is the starting line for Monday's KOSPI.

stories.hl: Delta cuts earnings outlook as fuel costs rise $6 billion
stories.dek: High oil prices have spread to airline earnings. The forecast for earnings per share was cut to $5.10–5.60.

popup.kick: Airlines · Energy · Press ✓ 2 outlets · figures are from the company's announcement
popup.title: Delta cuts earnings outlook as fuel costs rise $6 billion
popup.what: Delta Air Lines cut its outlook for this year, citing a $6 billion increase in fuel costs. Its adjusted earnings per share forecast fell to $5.10–5.60 from the earlier $6.50–7.50 (Reuters, The Globe and Mail). Fare increases could not make up for the higher fuel bill.
popup.why: A case of higher oil prices actually reaching corporate earnings. Fuel is a big share of airline costs, making airlines the first industry to react to oil.
popup.me: The effect could carry over to fuel surcharges and air fares. If you are planning overseas travel at year-end, consider when to book.
popup.say: The downgrade rests on the assumption that oil stays high for longer. If oil falls, it could move the other way. Other airlines' earnings reports are the point of comparison.
popup.src: Reuters, The Globe and Mail (company announcement, 10/9)

stories.kick: Industry · Semiconductors · Press ✓ 6 outlets · remarks are Chairman Chey's answers on site
stories.hl: SK's Chey Tae-won visits Honam chip site for the first time: “As fast as possible, at two-thirds the scale of Yongin”
body: SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won visited the Gwangju military airport, the planned site of the Honam semiconductor cluster, for the first time on the afternoon of the 9th. After touring the site with Jeonnam-Gwangju Mayor Min Hyung-bae and SK hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung, he said, “Once conditions allow us to build, we will build at the fastest speed possible” (Yonhap, Dong-A Ilbo, SBS). The site covers about 2.48 million pyeong (over 8.18 million m²). He also said he would build the fab first even if power and water supply are delayed (Dong-A Ilbo, Korea Economic Daily).

He said the plan is for a scale of “about two-thirds of Yongin at present,” which could grow if there is more land and demand (Kyunghyang Shinmun, ZDNet Korea). Some call it unusual for a group chairman to come to the site in person and speak about speed. But the groundbreaking date and the investment amount have not yet been announced, and power and water support, along with designation as a national industrial complex, remains up to the government and local authorities.

popup.title: SK's Chey Tae-won visits Honam chip site for the first time: “As fast as possible, at two-thirds the scale of Yongin”
popup.what: SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won visited the Gwangju military airport, the planned site of the Honam semiconductor cluster, on the afternoon of the 9th. He was accompanied by Jeonnam-Gwangju Mayor Min Hyung-bae, SK hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung and others. The site covers over 8.18 million m² (about 2.48 million pyeong) (Dong-A Ilbo). Chey said that once conditions allow, he would build as fast as possible, and said in effect that he would break ground first even if power and water supply are delayed (Dong-A Ilbo, Korea Economic Daily). He said the scale is planned at about two-thirds of Yongin at present, and could grow if there is more land and demand (Kyunghyang Shinmun, ZDNet Korea).
popup.why: The Honam semiconductor cluster has been politically contentious. Concern that investment in Yongin would shrink, and a dispute over whether companies actually want to go there, continued. The chairman stating his will at the site in person is a signal meant to ease that skepticism. But power and water are something a company cannot solve alone.
popup.me: It may affect local jobs and investment by partner firms. Because it is a facility with large power demand, it ties in the long run to discussions on electricity rates and the transmission grid.
popup.a: With AI memory demand surging, production bases have to grow. The chairman's visit is a promise to move fast.
popup.b: The words are fast, but the groundbreaking date and investment amount are not set. Whether the Yongin plan is affected needs more checking.
popup.say: ‘As fast as possible’ is attached to a conditional. Remember the proviso, ‘once conditions allow.’ What to watch next is the plan for power and water support and the schedule for designating a national industrial complex.
popup.src: Yonhap · Dong-A Ilbo · Kyunghyang Shinmun · SBS · Korea Economic Daily · Maeil Business Newspaper · ZDNet Korea (Chey's on-site remarks, 10/9)

stories.kick: Trade · Industry · Press ✓ 5 outlets · the size of the cut is the EU's explanation
stories.hl: China agrees with EU to cut hybrid vehicle exports; EU: “Roughly halved over four years”
body: On the 9th, China said it had reached agreement with the EU in trade talks on hybrid vehicles, and is also said to have agreed to ease export licensing for rare earths (Yonhap). The EU explained that the deal could cut Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the EU by roughly half over four years (The New York Times, Reuters). The two sides agreed to keep negotiating the electric-vehicle dispute.

The wording differs. China called it an ‘agreement’; Reuters and the Financial Times wrote ‘understanding.’ How the cuts, in effect a voluntary export restraint, will be made, and how far rare-earth licensing will be relaxed, has not been made public. For Korean carmakers that run into Chinese hybrids in Europe, it is news that could change the competitive landscape, but the impact can only be gauged once the details emerge.

popup.why: As sales of Chinese hybrids grew rapidly in Europe, the EU has been trying to limit imports. China holds a bargaining chip in rare-earth export licenses. What marks this deal is that it handled both issues together.

popup.b: Chinese makers could get around it with local production or other models. With the method of cuts undisclosed, it is too early to judge the effect.

stories.kick: Cyber · Finance · Press ✓ 5 outlets · the suspect's involvement is a security firm's analysis
stories.hl: Korean financial-sector hack: signs of links to Chinese AI tool and DDoS group; police expand investigation team to 43
body: Police recently expanded their investigation team on hacks of financial institutions to 43 people (Yonhap, Kyunghyang Shinmun). Security firm Logpresso analyzed that the person named as a suspect appears to have been active in a Chinese DDoS-for-hire group (Chosun Ilbo, Yonhap). According to Reuters, the developer of ARTEX, a Chinese AI security-testing tool reportedly used in the hacks, said it would take the source code private and stop updates (Dong-A Ilbo).

Reuters reported that nine domestic banks and two large churches are investigating whether an AI tool was used. In Japan, too, Daiwa Securities, SoftBank, Lawson and others have suffered successive cyber incidents. Yonhap pointed out that of 18 overseas-origin hacks since 2024, the attacker could not be identified in 16. Whether the named person is the actual attacker has not yet been confirmed. Customers are advised to turn on two-step verification in banking apps.

popup.kick: Cyber · Finance · Press ✓ 5 outlets · the suspect's involvement is a security firm's analysis
popup.title: Korean financial-sector hack: signs of links to Chinese AI tool and DDoS group; police expand investigation team to 43
popup.what: Police recently added digital forensics and international cooperation specialists to their financial-institution hacking investigation team, expanding it to 43 people (Yonhap, Kyunghyang Shinmun). Security firm Logpresso analyzed that the person named as a suspect appears to have been active in a Chinese DDoS-for-hire group (Chosun Ilbo). According to Reuters, the developer of ARTEX, a Chinese AI security-testing tool reportedly used in the hacks, said on GitHub that it would stop updates and take the source code private (citing Dong-A Ilbo). Yonhap reported that of 18 overseas-origin hacks since 2024, the attacker could not be identified in 16.
popup.why: AI tools have lowered the bar for hacking. Reuters reported that nine domestic banks and two large churches are investigating whether an AI tool was used, and that Daiwa Securities, SoftBank and Lawson in Japan also suffered incidents. The problem is a structure in which attackers are hard to identify.
popup.me: Change your banking app passwords and turn on two-step verification. Do not tap links in text messages impersonating financial firms. Confirmed damage is still limited to some institutions.
popup.a: Expanding the team and international cooperation are necessary steps. The reality is that identifying the attacker takes time.
popup.b: Some say the initial response was late. Police rebutted criticism of confusion over who leads the investigation and inadequate initial measures (Kyunghyang Shinmun).
popup.say: That the named person is the attacker is, so far, circumstantial. The tool's developer closing the code does not make code that has already spread disappear. What to watch next is the police's interim announcement and the financial authorities' inspection results.

The ICC. A permanent court that tries individuals for war crimes and crimes against humanity, located in The Hague, the Netherlands. It is a different body from the International Court of Justice, which handles disputes between states.

blocks.title: In brief
blocks.html:
• A ship passing through the Strait of Hormuz was hit by a projectile on the 9th, the UK Maritime Trade Operations said. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they would punish ships that stray from the shipping lane.Yonhap exclusive
  • Ukraine attacked a data center of Yandex, Russia's largest web portal, with drones for a second day. Yandex said a second facility was damaged.Yonhap, Reuters
  • U.S. prosecutors brought additional charges against Venezuela's former president Maduro, accusing him of torturing Americans. The pressure is continuing in court.Yonhap, AP
  • Pope Leo XIV approved Cardinal Tagle of the Philippines as dean of the College of Cardinals. It is the first time an Asian has held the post.AP, Reuters
  • Smoke haze from Indonesian wildfires has spread, closing schools in several Malaysian states. Two million students are affected.Yonhap, Reuters
  • The French government is deploying 3,000 substitute teachers to calm student protests. Protesters said they will keep fighting even after this first gain.Yonhap, Reuters
  • Canada's September employment unexpectedly fell and the unemployment rate edged up. The central bank, facing a rate decision, has more to worry about.Reuters and others
  • Netflix plans to cut about 5% of its staff, Puck News reported. It could be announced as early as next week. The company declined to comment.Reuters, CNA citing Puck News

blocks.title: Unverified — what we could not confirm
blocks.html:
“The U.S. will strike Iran intensively for three days.” There were reports of Defense Department planning and a brake applied by Trump, but Trump said there would be no attack before the November midterms. Nothing has been confirmed.

“Jung Chung-rae's visa hold is a sign of a crack in the Korea–U.S. alliance.” The visa is in ‘under review’ status, neither granted nor denied. The Foreign Ministry said it is inappropriate to link it to Korea–U.S. relations. The government also said “not true” to the claim that Secretary Lutnick had conveyed distrust of the National Intelligence Service.

“The financial-sector hacker is a member of a Chinese DDoS group.” Only circumstantial signs came out of a security firm's analysis. Police are investigating, and the attacker has not been determined.

blocks.title: What to watch today
blocks.html:
Sat 10/10 North Korea's Workers' Party founding anniversary. The pro baseball race for third place is in its final stretch. Domestic stock markets are closed for the weekend.

Weekend Developments on the Houthis and Hormuz, oil prices, and governments' reactions to the ICC sanctions. We also need to check Friday's New York close.

For readers The KOSPI opens Monday the 12th. Thursday's tech slide in New York and Friday's oil moves will all come in at once.
Glossary · dotted words — economics, law, security and science terms explained in the context of the story. The list grows every day.
DailyDrop · Source ✓ = primary document checked, Press ✓ = two or more independent outlets agree · 'Take' is DailyDrop's opinion We do not reprint article text. Summaries and sources only. · © 2026

International Criminal Court.d: A permanent international court that tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and the like. It sits in The Hague, the Netherlands. It is not a UN body; it runs on a treaty among its member states.
International Criminal Court.w: It is part of Pillay's record, and the U.S. has now sanctioned the court itself.

International Court of Justice.d: The UN's principal judicial organ, which settles disputes between states. Also called the ICJ. It hears cases against states, not individuals.
International Court of Justice.w: Pillay is an ad hoc judge there.

High Commissioner for Human Rights.d: The post that heads human rights work in the UN Secretariat. It monitors the human rights situation in each country and speaks out in criticism.

Houthis.d: An armed Shia group that controls northern Yemen. Backed by Iran, it has attacked Red Sea shipping and Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
Houthis.w: It claimed the attack on Riyadh airport.

Strait of Hormuz.d: A narrow waterway linking the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. A large share of the world's seaborne crude oil passes through it.
Strait of Hormuz.w: A ship was hit by a projectile on the 9th.

Revolutionary Guards.d: An Iranian military force separate from the regular army, answering directly to the supreme leader. It patrols the Strait of Hormuz and handles naval operations.
Revolutionary Guards.w: It said it would punish ships that stray from the shipping lane.

WTI.d: West Texas Intermediate crude. The benchmark for U.S. oil prices. It usually trades a few dollars below Brent.
WTI.w: It rose 3.6% on the 8th to the $91 range.

military airport.d: An airport used by military aircraft. Relocation of the Gwangju military airport is being pursued, and its site is mentioned as the planned location of the Honam semiconductor cluster.

fab.d: A factory that actually makes semiconductors. It needs clean rooms and large-scale power and water facilities.
fab.w: He said he would build the fab first even if power and water are late.

hybrid vehicles.d: Cars that use an engine and an electric motor together. With less charging burden than EVs, sales of Chinese ones have grown quickly in Europe.
hybrid vehicles.w: China agreed to cut its exports to the EU.

rare earths.d: 17 scarce metals used in EV motors, semiconductors and more. China accounts for most of the world's refining, so export licenses are used as a diplomatic card.
rare earths.w: China promised to ease export licensing.

DDoS.d: Distributed denial of service. An attack that paralyzes a server by sending connection requests from many devices at once.
DDoS.w: Signs emerged that the suspect was active in a DDoS-for-hire group.

spectrum.d: The radio bands used by wireless communication. States allocate them to operators, at very high prices.

parliamentary audit.d: The annual National Assembly oversight of government agencies' work. It runs for about a month in autumn.
parliamentary audit.w: Rep. Jung's attendance at the on-site audit in the Americas became difficult.

Gallup Korea.d: A polling firm that regularly surveys and publishes presidential approval.
Gallup Korea.w: It reported 37% positive evaluation of President Lee.

10-year Treasury yield.d: The yield on a 10-year government bond. The U.S. 10-year yield serves as the benchmark for long-term rates and global asset prices.

earnings per share.d: Net profit divided by the number of shares outstanding. The profit earned by one share of stock.
earnings per share.w: Delta cut its annual forecast to $5.10–5.60.

Norwegian Nobel Committee.d: The five-member body, appointed by the Norwegian Parliament, that chooses the Peace Prize laureate each year.
Norwegian Nobel Committee.w: It announced Pillay as the winner and its reasons.

ad hoc judge.d: At the International Court of Justice, a judge a party to a case may appoint for that case alone when the bench has no judge of its nationality.
ad hoc judge.w: Pillay sits on the ICJ in this capacity.

ICC.d: Short for the International Criminal Court, the permanent court in The Hague that tries individuals for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
ICC.w: The U.S. sanctioned the court itself.

ICJ.d: Short for the International Court of Justice, the UN's main judicial organ, which settles disputes between states.
ICJ.w: Pillay is an ad hoc judge there.

Mandela.d: Nelson Mandela, who became South Africa's first Black president after the end of apartheid and won the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize.
Mandela.w: Pillay is the first South African laureate since him.

Tomoko Akane.d: A Japanese judge who serves as president of the International Criminal Court.
Tomoko Akane.w: She was sanctioned by the U.S. in August, and Russia reportedly demanded her handover.

NHK.d: Japan's public broadcaster, funded mainly by viewer fees.
NHK.w: It reported the Treasury's designation of the ICC.

U.S. Treasury.d: The U.S. government department in charge of finances. Its Office of Foreign Assets Control administers and enforces sanctions lists.
U.S. Treasury.w: It announced the ICC's designation as a sanctions target.

Saudia.w: One of the dead at Riyadh airport was reported to be a Saudia captain.

UK Maritime Trade Operations.d: A center run by the British Royal Navy that gathers incident reports from merchant ships around the Red Sea, the Gulf and the Indian Ocean and warns shipping.
UK Maritime Trade Operations.w: It reported the projectile hit on a ship near Hormuz.

Starlink.d: SpaceX's satellite internet service, which uses thousands of low-orbit satellites to provide connections.
Starlink.w: The spectrum would underpin its mobile service.

Deutsche Telekom.d: Germany's largest telecom operator, which also controls the U.S. carrier T-Mobile.

Logpresso.w: Its analysis pointed to the suspect's links with a DDoS group.

ARTEX.d: The name of a Chinese AI-based security-testing tool, the kind of software meant to probe systems for weaknesses.
ARTEX.w: It reportedly was used in the hacks, and its developer said it would stop updates.

Yongin.d: A city in Gyeonggi Province near Seoul, where large semiconductor cluster plans are being pursued.
Yongin.w: Chey used its scale as the yardstick for the Honam site.

Nasdaq.d: A U.S. stock exchange and its index, heavily weighted toward technology companies.

S&P 500.d: A U.S. stock index tracking 500 large listed companies, widely used as a gauge of the overall market.

Yandex.d: Russia's largest internet company, known for its search engine and web portal.
Yandex.w: Its data center was attacked by drones for a second day.

Maduro.d: Nicolás Maduro, who led Venezuela from 2013 and has long faced criminal charges brought by U.S. prosecutors.
Maduro.w: Prosecutors added charges of torturing Americans.

Tagle.d: Luis Antonio Tagle, a cardinal from the Philippines.
Tagle.w: The pope approved him as dean of the College of Cardinals.

College of Cardinals.d: The body of all cardinals of the Catholic Church, who advise the pope and elect his successor. A dean heads it.
College of Cardinals.w: Tagle is the first Asian to lead it.

Workers' Party.d: North Korea's ruling party. It marks its founding anniversary on October 10.

Lutnick.d: Howard Lutnick, the U.S. Commerce Secretary.
Lutnick.w: A claim that he conveyed distrust of the National Intelligence Service was denied by the government.

National Intelligence Service.d: South Korea's intelligence agency, often abbreviated NIS.
National Intelligence Service.w: It appears in a claim the government called not true.

Democratic Party of Korea.d: One of South Korea's two largest parties, and the current ruling party.
Democratic Party of Korea.w: Rep. Jung belongs to it, and the party expressed regret over the visa hold.

midterms.d: U.S. congressional elections held midway through a president's four-year term, in November.
midterms.w: Trump said there would be no attack on Iran before them.

Honam.d: The southwestern region of South Korea, covering Gwangju and the Jeolla provinces.
Honam.w: The cluster is planned for this region.

voluntary export restraint.d: An arrangement in which an exporting country agrees to limit its own shipments, in place of the importer imposing tariffs or quotas.
voluntary export restraint.w: One side argues it is better than a tariff war.

two-step verification.d: A login method that asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, in addition to a password.
two-step verification.w: It is advised as protection after the financial-sector hacks.

national industrial complex.d: An industrial park the national government designates under law. Designation speeds up approvals and infrastructure support.
national industrial complex.w: The schedule for its designation is something to watch.

influencers.t: Trump shared a Truth Social post criticising the Nobel Peace Prize committee and the laureate.
Sampro TV posted an interview on whether US midterms and CPI will be turning points for the Korean stock market.
Saylor said he is optimistic about Elon Musk's vision for SpaceX, a possible tailwind for bitcoin (Benzinga).

President Lee Jae-myung used X on Hangeul Day to urge love of the Korean script (BBS).
